findings.title: Do not pipe unpinned remote script into sh at build time
findings.whyItBreaks: `curl -sL https://example.com/install.sh | sh` executes whatever bytes that URL serves (or now redirects to, due to `-L`) as root inside the build container with no version pin and no checksum/signature check. The content is fetched fresh on every build, so the image is non-reproducible and a compromised/renamed endpoint, DNS/MITM, or a hostile redirect yields arbitrary code execution in your build and any derived image. `-s` also hides curl diagnostics.

findings.title: Do not pipe unpinned remote script into sh at image build
findings.whyItBreaks: `curl -sL https://example.com/install.sh | sh` executes arbitrary remote content with no version pin, no integrity check, and no error propagation. The build is non-reproducible (the fetched bytes can change at any time) and any compromise/typosquat of that URL or its DNS/TLS path yields code execution baked into every image built from this Dockerfile. Additionally, `-s` suppresses errors and no `-f` is used, so an HTTP error page can be piped to `sh` and the pipeline's exit status reflects only `sh`, silently masking a failed download (swallowed failure signal).

findings.title: Do not pipe unverified remote script to sh in build
findings.whyItBreaks: `RUN curl -sL https://example.com/install.sh | sh` executes whatever the remote endpoint returns as root inside the image, with no content pin (no version/sha256) and no integrity check. A compromise or change of the remote script (or DNS/MITM of the fetch) yields arbitrary code execution in the build and any published image, and the build is non-reproducible because the fetched content is mutable.

findings.title: curl|sh swallows download failure, build can succeed silently
findings.whyItBreaks: `curl -sL` has no `-f`, so HTTP 4xx/5xx responses are treated as success with the error body written to stdout, and `-s` suppresses curl diagnostics. The shell stage is a bare `sh -c` with no `-e`/`pipefail`, so an empty, truncated, or HTML error body can be evaluated and the pipeline still exits 0. `RUN` therefore certifies the layer as successful even though the intended install did not run, silently shipping an image whose expected tooling is absent or partially installed.

findings.title: purgeProject deletes projects for non-admin users (authz bypass)
findings.whyItBreaks: Line 12 `if (user.isAdmin) return "forbidden";` drops the negation present in the base (`if (user.isAdmin && project.archived)`). Substituting real values: user.isAdmin=false + project.archived=true passes the line-12 guard (not admin, so no early return) and the line-13 guard (archived, so !archived is false), reaching `db.delete(project.id)` at line 14 and returning "purged". Any authenticated non-admin can therefore irreversibly purge/delete an archived project (data loss + privilege escalation). Conversely user.isAdmin=true now hits line 12 and returns "forbidden", so the previously-valid admin+archived purge is rejected. Both effects trace to the same missing `!`.

findings.title: Inverted isAdmin check allows non-admins to purge projects
findings.whyItBreaks: The base guard was `if (user.isAdmin && project.archived) { delete; return "purged" }`. The rewrite does `if (user.isAdmin) return "forbidden";`, which inverts the authorization: a non-admin (`isAdmin === false`) skips this branch, then the second guard `if (!project.archived)` also passes for a normal (non-archived) project, so `db.delete(project.id)` runs and returns "purged". Any non-admin caller can now permanently delete any non-archived project — an authentication/authorization bypass on a destructive path. Simultaneously a legitimate admin is now always rejected, a regression on the very action the function exists for.

findings.title: Cache key drops tenantId, leaking settings across tenants
findings.whyItBreaks: Before this PR the key was `${tenantId}:${name}`, so each tenant had an isolated cache entry. Now `const key = cacheKey(name)` produces `settings:${name}`, which is identical for every tenant. A call to `settingsFor(tenantA, "x", store)` populates `settings:x` with tenantA's fetched value; a subsequent `settingsFor(tenantB, "x", store)` returns that same cached value via `cache.get(key)` without ever calling `store.fetch(tenantB, ...)`. Tenant B (or any other tenant) therefore receives tenant A's setting value — a cross-tenant data disclosure and wrong-configuration/authorization bug (a per-tenant flag, quota, or secret material served to the wrong tenant). The same root cause makes `invalidate(name)` (line 20) delete the single shared key, so it can no longer invalidate one tenant's entry without evicting every tenant's, and it silently changed the exported `invalidate(tenantId, name)` signature.

findings.title: Cache key drops tenantId, leaking settings across tenants
findings.whyItBreaks: The module-level `cache` is shared by all tenants, but the key changed from `${tenantId}:${name}` to `cacheKey(name)` = `settings:${name}`, which no longer includes tenantId. `store.fetch(tenantId, name)` still reads per-tenant data, but the result is stored under a tenant-agnostic key (line 16) and returned on a cache hit without regard to tenantId (line 13). Once tenant A populates `settings:color`, every other tenant receives tenant A's value for `color` and store.fetch is never called for them — a cross-tenant configuration/secret disclosure. This is a live behavior regression on the exported `settingsFor` path.

findings.title: Restore tenantId to the settings cache key to prevent cross-tenant leaks
findings.whyItBreaks: Previously the key was `${tenantId}:${name}`, isolating entries per tenant. Now `cacheKey(name)` returns `settings:${name}`, dropping tenantId. `settingsFor(tenantA, 'x', store)` populates `settings:x`; a later `settingsFor(tenantB, 'x', store)` returns the cached hit at line 13 immediately, so tenant B receives tenant A's setting without ever calling `store.fetch(tenantB, 'x')`. This is a cross-tenant data disclosure and wrong-value regression. The same collision makes `invalidate(name)` (line 21) global rather than tenant-scoped, so invalidating one tenant's setting evicts/dirties it for every tenant.

findings.title: Make retryBackground surface terminal failure
findings.whyItBreaks: The new exported retryBackground returns void whether fn() succeeds on the first attempt or every attempt throws: the catch blocks (lines 27-29) discard each error and the function returns normally (undefined) after exhausting config.retries. Callers cannot distinguish success from total failure, so a background caller can report/mark the work as complete while nothing ran. Because it is an exported void API, every eventual caller is forced to conflate failure with success (the contract itself is the defect, no in-repo caller required).

findings.title: Alias/restore renamed timeoutMs field to stop breaking callers
findings.whyItBreaks: Config.timeoutMs was renamed to `timeout` (line 4) with no compatibility alias. Type-checked callers still passing timeoutMs now fail to compile. Callers not type-checked (plain JS) silently get config.timeout === undefined, so line 8/21 computes `Date.now() + undefined` = NaN, and the guard `Date.now() > deadline` (lines 10 and 23) is always false because any comparison with NaN is false. The timeout is therefore silently disabled and the loop runs every attempt. The rename also strips the 'ms' unit hint even though the value is still added to Date.now() as milliseconds, so a caller supplying seconds gets a ~1000x shorter timeout.

findings.title: retryBackground ignores maxAttempts and no-ops when retries is 0
findings.whyItBreaks: Config now exposes both maxAttempts and retries, but retryBackground bounds only with config.retries. A conventional retries=0 configuration (attempt once, retry zero times) performs no fn() call at all, and retries=N performs N total attempts instead of the expected 1+N; maxAttempts is silently ignored, so callers cannot control this function the way they do retry().

findings.title: Renaming timeoutMs to timeout breaks existing callers
findings.whyItBreaks: Config is exported, so removing timeoutMs and adding timeout/retries is a breaking public-API change. Existing TypeScript callers passing {maxAttempts, timeoutMs} fail to compile; any stale/untyped caller passes timeout=undefined, making deadline NaN at line 8, so 'Date.now() > deadline' is always false and the time budget for retry() and retryBackground() is silently disabled rather than used.

findings.title: retryBackground swallows every exhausted failure as void
findings.whyItBreaks: The new exported retryBackground catches every thrown error, continues, and finally returns void with no error, status, or attempt count. Callers cannot distinguish 'fn succeeded' from 'all attempts failed', even though the function is public; the failure signal previously propagating from fn's invocation is discarded at the catch.

findings.title: Config rename timeoutMs->timeout silently disables the deadline
findings.whyItBreaks: The exported public `Config` interface drops `timeoutMs` and adds `timeout`. Existing consumers (compiled JS, JSON/spread-built configs, or any caller not recompiled) that still pass `timeoutMs` leave `config.timeout` undefined at src/retry.ts:8, so `deadline = Date.now() + undefined = NaN`. The guard `if (Date.now() > deadline) return;` at src/retry.ts:10 is then always false (`x > NaN` is false), so the deadline never triggers and the loop runs to `maxAttempts` regardless of the configured timeout — silent loss of the retry timeout contract rather than a loud failure.

findings.title: retryBackground swallows the final failure as a void return
findings.whyItBreaks: The newly added, exported `retryBackground` catches every error with an empty `catch { continue; }` (src/retry.ts:27-28) and, when all attempts fail, falls out of the loop and returns `void` (src/retry.ts:30). Callers cannot distinguish 'fn eventually succeeded' from 'every attempt threw' — the last error is discarded with no propagation or logging, so failure is indistinguishable from the normal success value and may be reported/persisted as real.

findings.title: Stop silently fabricating findings in normalizeFinding
findings.whyItBreaks: The old body threw on every malformed field (invalid severity/category, missing file/title/whyItBreaks/suggestedFix); normalizeReview(strict=false) additionally caught those throws and dropped the finding. The new body maps every failure to a default instead: invalid severity -> "P1" (highest-severity-looking), invalid category -> "bug", missing title -> "Untitled finding", missing file -> "". A caller can no longer distinguish a malformed finding from a real one and will surface fabricated P1 findings with empty file/whyItBreaks/suggestedFix to the user. This is an exported (public) function, so the unusable contract is the defect even without an in-repo caller. This is TRIGGER D (failure mapped to a default value).

findings.title: Restore finite/positive guard for lineStart and lineEnd
findings.whyItBreaks: The removed guard `Number.isFinite(x) && x > 0` previously rejected bogus anchors. Now `Number(raw.lineStart ?? 0)` yields 0 for a missing value and NaN for non-numeric input (e.g. "abc"), and `lineEnd` falls back to 0 as well. NaN is still typed as `number`, so it passes the `Finding` contract, then serializes to `null` via JSON.stringify, and 0 anchors point at line 0. Findings therefore carry invalid line anchors where they were previously rejected.

findings.title: Restore validation: normalizeFinding swallows malformed findings
findings.whyItBreaks: The base version threw for invalid severity/category, missing file/title, and non-positive/non-finite line numbers; normalizeReview(strict=true, the default) propagated that error and normalizeReview(strict=false) dropped bad entries. The head version replaces every invalid field with a fabricated default (severity→"P1", category→"bug", file→"", lineStart→0, lineEnd→0/NaN) and normalizeReview now unconditionally does raw.findings.map(normalizeFinding) (line 131), so a malformed model output is emitted as a genuine-looking P1/bug finding with an empty file and line 0 instead of surfacing the failure. The caller of normalizeReview can no longer distinguish 'output was malformed' from 'the model reported a real P1 finding' — exactly the failure-vs-value conflation Trigger D covers. Two concrete wrong values: (a) any unrecognized severity (e.g. a typo'd critical/low value) is silently promoted to P1, fabricating a high-severity finding; (b) category is not trimmed/case-folded like severity is, so a meaningful value such as "Security" or " security" fails the CATEGORIES.includes check and is silently reclassified as "bug", dropping the security classification. A missing/invalid lineStart also yields NaN via Number() with no isFinite guard, which flows into Finding.lineStart.

findings.title: Reject malformed findings instead of silently defaulting them
findings.whyItBreaks: Every validation throw was removed from normalizeFinding, so malformed input is coerced to a plausible-looking Finding: an invalid/unknown severity becomes a real "P1" (line 98), category falls back to "bug" (lines 100-102), file/whyItBreaks/suggestedFix become empty strings (lines 103,107,108), and lineStart/lineEnd become 0 or NaN (lines 104-105). normalizeReview also dropped its strict handling (line 131) and its `strict` parameter (line 113), so it can no longer either throw (previous default strict=true) or drop bad findings (previous strict=false). A consumer that relied on the throw to detect and reject/retry malformed model output now silently ships fabricated findings — and failure is indistinguishable from a legitimate value, with garbage elevated to P1 severity. Exported public API with no in-repo callers, so the unusable contract itself is the defect.

findings.title: workflow_dispatch manual trigger no longer resolves PR head/base
findings.whyItBreaks: The job still permits manual runs (`if: github.event_name == 'workflow_dispatch' ...`, review.yml:24) and still accepts the required `pr_number` input (review.yml:10-14). On a workflow_dispatch event there is no `github.event.pull_request` context, so every `github.event.pull_request.*` expression evaluates to empty. Previously the deleted 'Resolve PR refs' step detected this (`if [ -n "$EVENT_HEAD" ]` else-branch) and populated head/base/base_ref via `gh pr view "$PR_NUM"`. Now: (1) checkout ref `github.event.pull_request.head.sha || github.ref` (review.yml:29) falls back to `github.ref`, i.e. the branch selected at dispatch (normally the default branch), so the tree under review is the wrong code; (2) `PR_BASE_SHA`/`PR_HEAD_SHA` (review.yml:45-46) become empty strings, so the CLI at review.yml:47 runs `--github --pr <n>` with no head/base SHAs; (3) `BASE_REF` falls back to the hardcoded 'main' (review.yml:35), which also fails if the default branch is not 'main'. Net effect: manual (bypass-webhook) review runs no longer review the requested PR and lose their SHA inputs.

findings.title: Manual dispatch checks out default ref, not the PR head
findings.whyItBreaks: On workflow_dispatch `github.event.pull_request` is absent, so `github.event.pull_request.head.sha` is empty and this ref falls back to `github.ref` (the branch selected at dispatch, normally the default branch) instead of the head of the PR named by the required `pr_number` input (line 12). The deleted 'Resolve PR refs' step used `gh pr view <PR_NUM> --json headRefOid ...` precisely to supply that head. Per the file's own comment (lines 3-5) 'the PR checkout's own src/ is the tool', so the manual path now installs/runs the default-branch tool and reviews the wrong revision; the `pr_number` input no longer influences the checkout. The 'Fetch base branch' step (lines 33-35) compounds this by hardcoding BASE_REF to 'main' on dispatch, so a PR whose base is not 'main' fetches the wrong base.

findings.title: Manual dispatch passes empty PR_BASE_SHA/PR_HEAD_SHA
findings.whyItBreaks: For workflow_dispatch (explicitly supported by `if: github.event_name == 'workflow_dispatch' ...` at line 24 and by the `pr_number` input at line 12 plus the `--pr ${{ github.event.inputs.pr_number || ... }}` fallback at line 47), `github.event.pull_request` is empty, so `github.event.pull_request.base.sha` and `.head.sha` both expand to empty strings. The removed `Resolve PR refs` step previously filled these via `gh pr view "$PR_NUM" --json headRefOid/baseRefOid`. A manual run now exports PR_BASE_SHA= and PR_HEAD_SHA=, so the review tool cannot resolve the base/head range it is asked to review.

findings.title: Manual dispatch checks out wrong ref and fetches 'main' base
findings.whyItBreaks: On workflow_dispatch `github.event.pull_request.head.sha` is empty, so line 29's `ref: ${{ github.event.pull_request.head.sha || github.ref }}` falls back to `github.ref` (the branch/dispatch ref), not the PR head requested via `pr_number`. Likewise line 35's `BASE_REF: ${{ github.event.pull_request.base.ref || 'main' }}` defaults to `main` regardless of the PR's actual base branch. The old step resolved both from `gh pr view`. The self-hosted job then runs `pnpm install` and `tsx src/cli.ts` against the wrong commit/branch, so a manual review produces a diff and results for the wrong code.

findings.title: Review-failure check downgraded to neutral, fail-opening the gate
findings.whyItBreaks: The catch block for a failed review now posts the check-run conclusion as "neutral" (was "failure"). GitHub branch protection treats a required status check as satisfied when its conclusion is success, neutral, or skipped, so a review that errored no longer blocks the PR, contradicting the summary it still sends ("Review errored and did NOT pass this PR"). It also makes a crashed review indistinguishable at the conclusion level from the legitimate `needs_human` verdict, which maps to neutral at VERDICT_CONCLUSION (src/adapters/github.ts:53), so automated consumers can no longer tell 'review crashed' from 'review ran and wants a human'.

findings.title: Review-error check now posts 'neutral', no longer blocks merge
findings.whyItBreaks: In the catch path, postCheck is now called with conclusion "neutral" instead of "failure". GitHub's required status checks treat conclusions success, neutral, and skipped as passing, so when review() throws the Needlefish check no longer blocks the PR — a PR can merge with no successful review. The very summary passed to postCheck still says 'Review errored and did NOT pass this PR', so the reported status contradicts the signal, and the previous "failure" value was the blocking one.

findings.title: Revert errored-review check conclusion from neutral to failure
findings.whyItBreaks: This is the catch block for a review that threw, and postCheck() posts the status check named "Needlefish" that gates the PR. Changing the conclusion from "failure" to "neutral" downgrades the failure signal: GitHub treats a `neutral` check-run conclusion as passing for required status checks, and the Checks UI renders it as a gray dot rather than a failed check. So when `review(bundle)` (or postReview) errors, the very check meant to block the PR now reports a non-failing state, while the check's own summary still says "Review errored and did NOT pass this PR" — the message and the machine verdict now contradict each other. A transient model/API failure (e.g. an induced outage) shifts from "blocked" to "does not block".
